Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Use the population-intervention-comparison-outcome framework to understand clinical
outcomes research.
Explain the utility of patient-reported outcome measures in evaluating patient outcomes.
Compare and contrast the various forms of economic analysis using cost and clinical
outcomes.
Introduction

Demand for sound research rather than expert opinion to form the basis of clinical
decision making in the field of orthopaedic traumatology continues to increase. In the
past decade, an unprecedented investment in high-quality multicenter clinical studies
has occurred. At the same time, academic pressure to publish research in the ever-
increasing number of journals has led to a similar or greater increase in the volume of
low-quality studies.1,2 Regardless whether orthopaedic traumatologists desires to
become actively involved in clinical investigation or simply to interpret the growing body
of medical literature, they must have an understanding of research methodology and
the instruments used to report outcomes. The use of clinical outcome instruments as a
quality metric appears to be increasing and may be linked to physician reimbursement
in the future.3,4 Several outcome instruments are used in orthopaedic trauma, and the
introduction of new instruments is likely to increase in the future5 (Resource 1).
Population-Intervention-Comparison-Outcome Framework
The population-intervention-comparison-outcome (PICO) framework is used to highlight
principles of clinical outcomes research.
Population
Use the reported inclusion criteria to outline the characteristics of the population being
studied.
Eligibility criteria affect the heterogeneity of a study population. Homogenous study
populations provide less variability but may be difficult to obtain.
Broader eligibility criteria may increase the external validity (generalizability) of study findings
but may obscure smaller findings.
The AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association fracture classification provides well-
defined definitions commonly used for studies involving patients fractures.

Population
The first step in developing a research question is to define the patient population being
studied. The sample of patients enrolled is critical to establishing to whom study results
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
2/26

pertain. The eligibility criteria, as described in the methods section of a published
research article, typically include patient age range, injury characteristics, time period,
location, and other key characteristics. As criteria specificity increases, the study
population becomes more homogeneous, and the resulting outcomes may have
decreased variability; however, stringent eligibility criteria may make adequate sample
size difficult to achieve. In addition, study results may become difficult to generalize to a
broader patient population. More pragmatic clinical trial designs with inclusive eligibility
criteria are becoming more common and may have more generalizable conclusions.6,7
Intervention and Comparison
Within the PICO framework, the new treatment option typically is considered the intervention.
It may be any form of treatment (eg, surgical, nonsurgical, medication, rehabilitation protocol).
The standard of treatment is considered the baseline (also called the comparator).
Methods for assigning patients to an intervention should be closely scrutinized as a source of
potential bias.
Confounding bias occurs if one group has fundamental differences associated with the
outcome.
Study designs to reduce confounding bias include randomization, matching, and restriction.
Statistical methods to reduce confounding bias include stratification and regression analysis.

Intervention and Comparison
Hypothesis-driven research often compares two or more interventions or treatment
strategies. Within the PICO framework, the new treatment typically is called the
intervention, and the standard of treatment is called the baseline (also called the
comparator).
The method of assigning patients to a treatment is a key component of the study design.
In an ideal experimental model, every participant would receive the intervention, and the
comparison treatment and would serve as a perfect internal control. Because this ideal
usually is not possible, studies are designed to create patient groups that are as similar
to one another as possible. The preferred standard method is random assignment to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
3/26

treatment, typically via sealed envelopes or a computer program. Some methods, such
as assigning a treatment via a medical record number, allow assignments to be
predicted and can introduce a patient selection bias; the use of such a method is called
pseudo-randomization. Randomization can occur at an individual or group level.
Randomization of groups, or cluster randomization, is a common feature of pragmatic
clinical trials (trials that are conducted in active clinical practice). These trials can achieve
larger sample sizes and are more generalizable than results from more individually
randomized clinical trials conducted in a controlled experimental setting (known as
explanatory clinical trials).6,7
Study designs that do not assign treatments according to an experimental protocol but
rather by provider preference or an existing clinical protocol are considered to be
observational. Treatment groups in an observational study may have important
differences associated with the outcome, which may lead to confounding bias. In
fracture studies, injury severity is a common source of this type of bias. The selected
treatment often differs based on injury severity, and severe injuries, by their nature, are
associated with poorer outcomes. A key characteristic of a confounder is that it is
associated with the exposure (intervention) and the outcome.
In addition to randomization, study design features that can be used to prevent
confounding include matching and restriction. In matching, patients in the intervention
and comparison groups are selected based on shared characteristics that may lead to
confounding, such as age or injury severity. For example, each patient with diabetes
mellitus who is assigned to the intervention is matched with a patient with diabetes
mellitus who is assigned to the comparison treatment. The restriction strategy is similar
to matching except that patients are simply excluded from the study if they do not fall
within the specified range of potentially confounding variables. In the example,
restriction would be achieved by excluding all patients with diabetes mellitus. The
disadvantages of the matching and restriction strategies are that sample sizes are
limited, the between-group effect of the confounding variables cannot be compared, and
unknown or unmeasured confounders cannot be accounted for.
Statistical methods also can be used to control for confounding after a study is
completed. Stratification divides the study subjects into subgroups defined by potential
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
4/26

confounding variables. The effect of the intervention is assessed within each
homogeneous subgroup, and the effects are pooled using a statistical weighting method,
such as the Mantel-Haenszel test.8 Alternatively, confounding can be accounted for by
conducting a multivariate logistic regression analysis that computes a unique odds ratio
for each variable included in the model. Both of these methods can control only for
measured confounders. This limitation affects all methods to reduce confounding, with
the exception of randomization. Randomization creates equivalent groups even with
respect to confounders that cannot be predicted or measured in advance.
The timing of data collection with respect to the intervention and outcome is another
important distinction in categorizing research studies. Studies that begin collecting data
before the outcome has occurred are considered prospective. Researchers first enroll
patients in the study and then wait for the outcome to occur. Conversely, retrospective
studies are initiated after the outcome has occurred. Data often are obtained from
medical records, and the quality of the data may be limited because many variables are
not recorded or are inaccurately recorded. By definition, a retrospective study always is
observational because patients were assigned to the treatment group before the study
was initiated.
Outcomes
Many factors affect a patient’s overall health-related quality of life (HRQOL); however, only
some may be affected by any given intervention.
Clinical research relies on various instruments to evaluate outcomes; disease-specific or body
region–specific instruments may be more sensitive to change yet lack the comparability across
health conditions assessed via general health measures.
Selected outcome measures should correlate with the clinical question being posed. A
combination of instruments, including disease-specific, general, and performance-based
outcomes, may be required.

Outcomes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
5/26

Various potential outcome measures that can be selected for a clinical research study
may make it difficult to select the best instrument and understand its interpretation. The
Wilson-Cleary conceptual framework for evaluating outcome measurements considers
the pathway from a patient’s underlying altered physiology to mental and physical
symptoms to overall HRQOL.9 Opportunities for measurement exist at each step along
the pathway. For example, at one end of the spectrum is plain radiography, which
commonly is used in trauma studies to assess bony healing and alignment even though
radiographic measures of alignment may not be correlated with a patient’s subjective
experience of pain or functional ability. Moving toward the other end of the spectrum,
outcome measures such as a pain scale, strength, or range-of-motion testing may not
correlate with a patient’s overall HRQOL. Clinician- or surgeon-centered outcomes tend
to differ from patient-reported outcomes (PROs), and an increasing emphasis is being
placed on PROs in clinical research. Instruments that measure HRQOL can be affected by
an unrelated medical or nonmedical factor, such as comorbidities or psychosocial
support. In addition, these instruments often do not explain identified differences in
HRQOL. For example, an intervention for a fracture may demonstrate an improvement
in HRQOL; however, whether the improvement is attributable to the patient’s healing
rate, limb alignment, or self-efficacy remains unanswered. Only by measuring outcomes
across the spectrum can this question be answered. Therefore, investigators should
consider administering PROs that measure HRQOL in combination with other outcome
measures across the outcomes spectrum.
Clinical End Points
Bony Union
Fracture union occurs across a continuum rather than as a discrete event.
Several scoring systems have been evaluated to more objectively measure and report fracture
union, including the Radiographic Union Score for Tibial Fractures (RUST), modified RUST, and
Radiographic Union Scale for the Hip scores.

Bony Union
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
6/26

Bony union is one of the primary goals of fracture management. Because fracture union
is a process that occurs across a continuum rather than as a discrete event, it may be
problematic to use bony union as the primary end point of a research study.10,11 Union
has been defined as an event ranging from painless weight bearing to bridging of three
of four cortices on orthogonal plain radiographs; however, the reliability of these
assessments is poor.10 The RUST is a relatively new measurement based on assessment
of cortical bridging.12,13 Each cortex (medial, lateral, anterior, and posterior) is assessed
and assigned a point value: 1 = fracture line, no callus; 2 = fracture line, visible callus; 3 =
no fracture line, bridging callus. The total score of the four cortices, ranging from 4 to 12,
may represent the continuous nature of fracture healing, and the reliability of the RUST
score was found to be better than the bridging of three of four cortices or orthopaedic
surgeons’ subjective impressions of union.14 The RUST score has been modified to a
four-level assessment of each cortex (modified RUST) and validated for use for the tibia
and femur.15 In addition, the Radiographic Union Scale for the Hip is a validated method
for assessing healing of femoral neck and intertrochanteric hip fractures.16,17
Revision Surgery
Revision surgery is a common end point in orthopaedic research.
Clearly defined criteria for revision surgery and independent adjudication committees can
reduce the bias that results from individual provider decision making.

Revision Surgery
Revision surgery is another clinical end point that is relevant to patients.18 Mortality may
not be substantially affected by orthopaedic management, and revision surgery offers an
alternative objective end point to differentiate between fracture interventions. The
common criticism of revision surgery as an outcome is that it relies on the subjective
assessment of the treating surgeon. This objection can be overcome by strictly defining
the criteria for revision surgery. Large studies often use an independent adjudication
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
7/26

committee to assess whether the criteria for revision surgery have been met for each
patient.19
Functional Outcomes
Timed-Up-and-Go Test
Measures number of seconds required for a subject to stand from a seated position, walk 10
feet, and return to a seated position
Useful for assessing the functional capacity of geriatric patients

Timed-Up-and-Go Test
Most orthopaedic interventions are intended to improve function. Various outcome
instruments directly measure physical functioning and performance. Among the most
well-known of these is the Timed-Up-and-Go test, which measures the number of
seconds required for a subject to stand from a seated position, walk 10 feet, and return
to a seated position.20 This test is particularly useful for assessing the functional capacity
of older adults, and the results of the test, if administered soon after hemiarthroplasty
for femoral neck fracture, were correlated with the long-term outcomes.21
Wearable Activity Monitors
Can be passively and remotely collected from patients; growing availability among the trauma
population.
Preliminary data validate the utility of wearable activity monitors in the orthopaedic trauma
population.

Wearable Activity Monitors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
8/26

Wearable activity monitors that record physical activity provide a method for measuring
function that is increasingly available because of technologic improvements.
Pedometers, which record each step, have been in existence for centuries; however,
more advanced devices recently have gained popularity with consumers and
researchers.22 Accelerometers are similar in principle but can differentiate low- and
high-intensity activities. Modern accelerometers can detect movements in three-
dimensional space. The use of these devices in fracture studies has been limited;
however, as the technology is incorporated into smartphones and other wearable
devices, more data can be harnessed to measure outcomes.
Several studies have investigated the validity of these devices and applications,23,24
including preliminary studies examining their utility in orthopaedic trauma patients.25 In
other surgical domains, studies have found a correlation between lower device recorded
physical activity and postoperative complications, hospital length of stay, and patient-
reported outcome measures.25,26 Smartphone application-based activity trackers are as
accurate as dedicated wearable devices24 and provide more sustained outpatient
data.27
Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
Generic instruments attempt to capture a patient’s overall quality of life using a metric that is
comparable across various diseases.
Disease-specific instruments are designed to be more responsive for a particular clinical
scenario.
Selecting the appropriate instrument for a study is driven by factors, including validity,
reliability, and practicality of administration.

Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
Outcome questionnaires can be broadly categorized as generic or disease-specific.24
Generic instruments attempt to capture a patient’s overall quality of life using a metric
that is comparable across various diseases. Because these instruments must capture

desired by researchers studying a specific condition. Therefore, a large number of
disease-specific and body region–specific instruments have been developed and

Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form
Most widely used generic survey in medicine (Resource 5).
Provides a physical and mental component score, with higher scores indicating better health
Has been shortened to 12 items or 6 subsets, called the Medical Outcomes Study 12-Item
Short Form and Medical Outcomes Study Six-Dimension Short Form (SF-6D), respectively

Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form
The Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form (SF-36) was developed for the Medical
Outcomes Study, a cohort study performed in the 1980s that compared clinical
outcomes in different healthcare delivery systems.28 The SF-36 subsequently became
the most widely used generic survey in medicine.29 The 36 questions in eight domains
yield a physical component score and a mental component score. The SF-36 uses a
proprietary system, in which scores range from 0 to 100, with a mean of 50 and a
standard deviation of 10; a higher score reflects better health. To reduce the burden on
study subjects and improve the ease of administration, the Medical Outcomes Study 12-
Item Short Form was developed using a 12-item subset of the SF-36. The SF-6D, another
subset of the SF-36, uses 11 items from six domains of the full questionnaire. Dissimilar
from the SF-36 and the Medical Outcomes Study 12-Item Short Form, scores on the SF-
6D are correlated with utility, a concept from economic theory that attempts to quantify
an individual’s preference for a given health state from 0 to 1 (1 is perfect health, and 0 is
equivalent to death). These results are useful for economic analysis.
EQ-5D Health Survey
Generic health outcome survey
Five-item survey on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or
depression
Ceiling effects are common, which may make identification of differences difficult in high-
functioning populations.


EQ-5D Health Survey
The multinational EuroQol Group developed the EQ-5D instrument in the 1980s as a
short, practical questionnaire that can accurately estimate an individual’s quality of life.30
The EQ-5D is considerably shorter than many other generic surveys; it has only five
questions on mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or
depression. Similar to the SF-6D, the EQ-5D assigns a health state value. This is a
numeric value that can be used in further analyses, such as a cost-effectiveness analysis.
Therefore, the EQ-5D is a useful instrument if economic analysis is planned; however,
ceiling effects are common, which may make the identification of differences difficult in
high-functioning populations. The EQ-5D has been problematic in differentiating
outcomes from musculoskeletal problems involving the upper extremity.31
Musculoskeletal Function Assessment
Generic instrument for evaluating musculoskeletal conditions
Full and short versions available (110 items versus 46 items, respectively)

Musculoskeletal Function Assessment
The Musculoskeletal Function Assessment (MFA) commonly is used in orthopaedic
studies as a generic instrument for evaluating musculoskeletal conditions. The full MFA
has 110 items, and the Short Musculoskeletal Function Assessment (SMFA) has 46
items32 (Resource 6). The ease of administering the SMFA compared with the MFA has
led to it becoming the more commonly selected measure in fracture studies.33 However,
in the Study to Prospectively Evaluate Reamed Intramedullary Nails in Patients with Tibial
Fractures, which evaluated reamed and unreamed nails for tibial shaft fractures, the
SMFA did not add any information beyond that provided by the SF-36, and the
researchers concluded that using the generic instrument was preferred to allow for
broad comparisons across disease states, at least in patients with a tibial shaft
fracture.34

The process of selecting the appropriate instrument for a study is driven by factors such
as validity, reliability, and practicality of administration. Validity is related to the content
of the questionnaire and the ability of the survey to appropriately reflect changes in the
study participants. Ideally, studies use instruments previously found to be valid for the
study population. Reliability refers to the precision and reproducibility of an instrument.
Practicality includes factors such as the length of time required to complete the
questionnaire. The properties of several of generic instruments are outlined in Table 2.

Sickness Impact Profile
The Sickness Impact Profile (SIP) is a generic instrument that was developed in the 1970s to
quantify an individual’s quality of life by assessing his or her ability to perform daily activities.35

Sickness Impact Profile
The survey consists of 136 questions in a yes-or-no format; the final score is derived
from the percentage of affirmative answers. The 12 domains of the SIP are ambulation,
mobility, body care and movement, social interaction, alertness behavior, emotional
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
15/26

behavior, communication, sleep and rest, eating, work, home management, and
recreation and pastimes. The Lower Extremity Assessment Project used the SIP as the
primary outcome measure and found no substantial between-group differences in the
scores of patients with a severe lower extremity injury who were treated via amputation
or limb salvage; however, analysis of a subset of patients with foot and ankle trauma
revealed that those who required a free-tissue transfer or ankle fusion had poorer SIP
scores than those who required a below-knee amputation.36
Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System
National Institutes of Health–funded outcome instrument
Set of generic and specific instruments that may be administered as set length pen-and-paper
questionnaires or digitally via computerized adaptive testing (CAT).
CAT and item response theory are used to increase the efficiency and accuracy of reported
outcomes by tailoring the questionnaire based on patient responses. This reduces respondent
burden (Resource 7).

Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System
In response to the demand for PROs, the National Institutes of Health funded the
Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS), a multicenter
cooperative that developed an improved outcome instrument using technology and
psychometric theory.37,38
PROMIS is free to use and can be accessed via several methods. Analog versions of the
questionnaires are available on the National Institutes of Health PROMIS website. Digital
versions are available as integrated applications within electronic medical records, such
as Epic, and in research platforms such as REDCap. Stand-alone applications can be
accessed via mobile and web-based platforms.
PROMIS is unique in that it allows items to be selected from several different item banks,
each developed to measure a specific domain, such as extremity function or pain.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outcomes of Musculoskeletal Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003019
16/26

Domains can be further profiled to physical, mental, and social health. PROMIS
measures can be administered in three different manners: short-form assessments
using a static subset of a domain’s item bank, CAT for a specific domain, or profile option
in which all items are completed for a specific domain. Item response theory and CAT
are two key features that affect the administration of PROMIS and distinguish it from
common legacy instruments for measuring HRQOL that are static. In item response
theory, the response to a question determines the next question to be administered.
This feature increases the efficiency and accuracy of the final score; by using computer
adaptive testing, PROMIS can achieve the same validity and reliability as conventional
techniques using fewer questions. For patients with orthopaedic trauma, the testing
time for the PROMIS physical function domain was 44 seconds compared with 599
seconds for the SMFA.39 In addition, no ceiling effects were reported for PROMIS
compared with a 14% ceiling effect for the SMFA. Ceiling and floor effects occur if an
instrument cannot differentiate individuals at the high (ceiling) or low (floor) end of the
scale. Because PROMIS uses item response theory to choose each question based on the
response to the preceding question, it can focus on demanding activities for high-
functioning subjects and reduce the ceiling effect. The ceiling effect has been particularly
problematic for generic instruments used to assess patients with an upper extremity
injury.32 PROMIS is superior to the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand score,
which was designed for patients with an upper extremity injury.37
Despite theoretic and practical advantages, PROMIS continues to lag behind legacy
instruments in the assessment of quality of life in orthopaedic trauma studies. A recent
review of 319 orthopaedic trauma clinical studies published between 2014 and 2018
found that PROMIS, including PROMIS Physical Function, Pain Interference, and Upper
Extremity Function, was used in only 7 patients (2%).
Improved familiarity and interpretability of PROMIS, via initiatives such as PROsetta
Stone, which aim to improve comparability with legacy instruments, likely will increase
its adoption in clinical and research settings. Lack of widespread use in the orthopaedic
literature lends to the primary limitations of PROMIS. These limitations include how
PROMIS scores correlate with historically recorded legacy instrument scores and
databases and the utility of PROMIS across all orthopaedic patient populations (Video 1).

Economic Analysis

Economic Analysis
In combination with the expanding emphasis on improving quality in health care by
measuring PROs, pressure to reduce costs is increasing. In the future, surgeons will need
to be familiar with the nomenclature of economic analysis and quantitative research
methods used to estimate the value of medical interventions in health care. Cost
analysis is an increasingly important aspect of comparative effectiveness research and
accompanies many large prospective studies in orthopaedic trauma care and other
areas of medical practice.

A simple comparison of the total cost of two interventions is called a cost-minimization or cost
analysis (eg, comparing the cost of two implants that are believed to result in an equivalent
clinical outcome).

Cost-Minimization Analysis
This type of study is appropriate if the clinical benefits of each treatment strategy are not
substantially different. In this uncommon situation, the cost-minimization study design is
straightforward and may inform a subsequent, more complex economic analysis.
Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) attempts to estimate the cost of a given healthcare
intervention to produce a unit of health benefit.38

Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Usually, the results of a CEA are quantitatively expressed as the ratio of the cost of the
intervention to some term that quantifies the benefit. The numerator always contains
cost, whereas the denominator may be any outcome of interest. For example, a CEA may
report the cost per life saved or the cost per complication averted. The disadvantage of
this method is that the more specific the outcome selected for the denominator, the
more difficult it is to make comparisons across studies.
Cost-Utility Analysis
Estimates the cost of a given healthcare intervention to produce a measure of utility, most
commonly quality-adjusted life year
More specific type of analysis that allows for closer comparison of treatment options; the
incremental cost-effectiveness ratio is a comparison between the studied intervention and a
chosen baseline comparator.


Cost-Utility Analysis
Under the umbrella of CEA is cost-utility analysis, which is a more specific type of
economic analysis. Rather than a clinical outcome, the denominator of the ratio is utility,
which expresses the societal preference for a health state, ranging from 1 (equating to
perfect health) to 0 (equating to death).40 For example, a patient with severe
osteoarthritis might have a utility of 0.7, and a patient with a spinal cord injury may have
a utility of 0.3. By multiplying the utility of the health state by the number of years spent
in the health state, quality-adjusted life years can be calculated. This method makes
comparisons between a single metric intervention that prolongs life and those that have
more of an effect on the quality of life possible. Quality-adjusted life years are the
recommended and most commonly used value for the denominator of a cost-utility
analysis.40
The primary outcome in a cost-utility analysis is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio,
which is a ratio of the incremental cost of the intervention to the comparator and the
incremental utility of the intervention relative to the comparator40:
Studies must include a baseline comparison to report an accurate incremental cost-
effectiveness ratio rather than assuming that the baseline cost and utility are zero. Even
a do-nothing approach has a cost and health effect on the population and, therefore,
should be estimated as the comparator. In fracture healing studies, the comparator
typically is nonsurgical management, which often is associated with the cost of clinic
visits for cast immobilization and radiographs and will have an outcome that is almost
invariably better than zero, which is equivalent to death.
Cost-Benefit Analysis
Converts cost and benefit into monetary units expressed as a net monetary benefit (NMB)
Requires assigning monetary value to patient outcomes


Cost-Benefit Analysis
Dissimilar from CEA or cost-utility analysis, in which the cost and benefit are kept
separate by using a ratio, a cost-benefit analysis, or benefit-cost analysis, converts cost
and benefit into monetary units. The result can be expressed as the NMB. An NMB
higher than zero indicates that the strategy will save money, and an NMB lower than
zero indicates that the strategy will lose money. The challenge of this approach is that
ethical issues arise if a monetary value is assigned to human life or health benefits.
Therefore, benefit-cost analysis infrequently is used in health care. The principal
advantage of this approach at a governmental level is that it can be used to compare
programs in other sectors, such as education or environment relative to healthcare
programs.
Summary
The PICO framework is a useful tool for constructing and interpreting clinical research studies.
Patient outcomes can be assessed via many metrics, both self-reported and passively
collected.
Patient-reported outcome measures may be generic or disease/condition specific. If used
appropriately, patient-reported outcome measures can help evaluate health status.
Economic analysis is an increasingly important aspect of outcome analysis.
Accurate measure of patient outcomes in combination with economic analysis may help
inform clinical care, research, and health policy.
